title: Infra GPU Fleet Capacity, IaC Modules, and CI/CD Playbook
author: Sofia Ramirez
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates guidance for operating Redwood's GPU fleet and capacity planning, the Terraform/IaC module patterns we use, and our CI/CD and build practices. It is intended for infrastructure engineers, SREs, and runtime platform owners who make changes to capacity, networking, and IaC that affect inference availability and cost.

Goals and scope

- Provide a single reference for: GPU fleet topology, capacity thresholds, and scaling policies.
- Document required Terraform module interfaces and ownership patterns.
- Define CI/CD gating, validation, and rollout steps for infrastructure changes.
- Centralize runbook steps for common operational tasks (scale-up, node replacement, emergency rollback).

Ownership

- Primary owner: infra-engineering (team: Infra).
- Runtime & capacity: eng-serving-runtime (secondary).
- On-call escalation: eng-sre.
- Contact: #infra-oncall (Slack), PagerDuty escalation policy: "GPU-Fleet-Oncall".

Architecture and components (high level)

- fleet-manager: central control-plane service that tracks GPU pool health and schedules capacity adjustments.
- capacity-allocator: autoscaler that issues Terraform plan/apply requests or cloud API ops for burst pools.
- node-agent: lightweight daemon on GPU nodes for health, KV cache metrics, and lifecycle hooks.
- telemetry: Prometheus exporters + Grafana dashboards; logs to Loki; traces to Jaeger.
- IaC: Terraform modules (modules/gpu-pool, modules/networking, modules/cloud-accounts).
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions for Terraform plan + policy checks; Argo CD for runtime manifests; Terraform Cloud (TFC) used for state locking in production.

Capacity planning & SLOs

- Production SLOs (examples):
  - API P99 latency for inference requests: <= 350 ms (regional).
  - Time-to-first-token (model-dependent) tracked per model profile.
  - Fleet availability (nodes ready): 99.95% monthly.
  - Queue latency (request queued before scheduling): median < 50ms; 95th < 200ms.

- Capacity thresholds & alerts:
  - GPU_utilization > 85% sustained for 10m -> page to oncall.
  - pending_requests_count > 100 for 5m -> Sev2 alert.
  - node_eviction_rate > 0.5% in 1h -> investigate thermal/hardware issues.
  - free_capacity_ratio < 10% -> trigger capacity-allocator to provision burst pool.

- Overprovisioning strategy: Keep 15% headroom during business hours (08:00-20:00 PT) and 5% overnight. Adjust per-region based on historical peak factor.

Terraform/IaC modules (patterns and requirements)

- Module responsibilities (naming convention):
  1. modules/gpu-pool: create node groups, autoscaling groups, GPUAMI, node labels, taints, and node pool lifecycle policies.
  2. modules/networking: VPCs, subnets, route tables, security groups for inference subnets, NAT/IGW config.
  3. modules/cloud-accounts: IAM roles, KMS keys, billing tags, organization-level guardrails.
  4. modules/monitoring: Prometheus exporters, Alertmanager config, Grafana dashboards as code.

- Module interface contract (minimum):
  - inputs: name_prefix, region, instance_types (list), desired_capacity, min_capacity, max_capacity, subnet_ids, labels (map string->string), taints (list).
  - outputs: node_group_id, autoscaling_group_name, instance_profile_arn, node_pool_tags.

- Example usage snippet (Terraform, keep in repository modules-consumer):

  ```hcl
  module "gpu_pool_prod_east" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@internal-repo/infra/modules.git//gpu-pool?ref=v1.3.0"
    name_prefix = "gpu-prod-east"
    region = "us-east-1"
    instance_types = ["g5.12xlarge", "g5.8xlarge"]
    desired_capacity = 40
    min_capacity = 10
    max_capacity = 120
    subnet_ids = var.prod_subnet_ids
    labels = { role = "inference", pool = "prod-east" }
    taints = ["dedicated=inference:NoSchedule"]
  }
  ```

- Module review & release process:
  1. Change implemented in feature branch; include acceptance tests (terraform validate, tflint).
  2. Open PR: include changelog entry and upgrade notes.
  3. Reviewer required: module owner + infra-arch representative.
  4. Merge -> create module tag (semver) and publish in internal module registry.

CI/CD and Build practices

- Terraform flow:
  - Pull request triggers: terraform fmt, terraform validate, tflint, checkov (security policies).
  - PR must include plan output artifact.
  - Plan applies: Automated apply allowed only in non-prod workspaces. Production applies require:
    - Two approvers from infra-engineering or eng-arch.
    - Successful integration tests and policy checks.
  - Terraform Cloud used for state; service principals stored in Vault.

- Pipeline components:
  - GitHub Actions: pre-merge checks and integration test runners.
  - Argo CD: continuous delivery for Kubernetes manifests in runtime clusters.
  - Build images: Packer for GPU AMI builds; image pipeline publishes AMIs to shared account with immutability tags.

- CI gating & tests:
  1. Unit: terraform validate, tflint.
  2. Integration: apply to ephemeral environment (PR env) and run smoke tests (node pool creation, label/taint verification).
  3. Cost guardrails: diff analyzer flags changes that increase estimated monthly cost > $5k.
  4. Security policies (checkov): ensure no public S3, correct KMS usage, least-privilege IAM.

Runbooks (operational procedures)

1) Scale-up (proactive)

- When to run: traffic forecast > 70% of provisioned capacity for next 24h or oncall alert for utilization.
- Steps:
  1. Open internal change ticket with justification and target size.
  2. Update consumer Terraform variables (desired_capacity) in the appropriate workspace.
  3. Run `terraform plan -var-file=secrets/prod.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan` and attach plan to ticket.
  4. Request approvals (2) for prod apply.
  5. `terraform apply plan.tfplan` via Terraform Cloud or runbook automation.
  6. Validate: confirm new nodes in fleet-manager, check node_agent health, verify Prometheus metrics show new capacity registered.
  7. Monitor for 30 minutes for eviction, OOMs, or kernel panics.

2) Node replacement (hot swap)

- Use-case: kernel/hardware faults, GPU ECC errors, or maintenance.
- Steps:
  1. `kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data` (if k8s).
  2. Stop workload on node via fleet-manager maintenance API.
  3. Verify pods rescheduled and no long-running ephemeral disk writes.
  4. Terminate instance via cloud console or `aws ec2 terminate-instances` and allow ASG to recreate.
  5. Confirm node_agent registers and passes health checks.
  6. Remove node from maintenance.

3) Emergency rollback (Terraform)

- Trigger: apply caused scheduling regressions or production outage.
- Steps:
  1. Immediately scale down/scale-up to a safe known-good size using TFC run or cloud console to restore capacity.
  2. Revert the IaC change: revert the merge commit in GitHub and open revert PR.
  3. Apply previous Terraform state if necessary (consult eng-sre and infra-arch).
  4. Post-incident: run a postmortem and update this playbook with root cause and prevention.

Dashboards, alerts and monitoring

- Dashboards to maintain (examples):
  - GPU Fleet Overview: cluster-level GPU_utilization, per-pool capacity, pending queue length, average time-to-first-token.
  - Node Health: ECC errors, memory errors, temperature, fan speed, disk health.
  - Cost & Utilization: running instances per family, hourly spend, amortized per-token cost.

- Key alert thresholds (repeat for clarity):
  - P99 latency > 500ms for 5m -> Sev2.
  - GPU_utilization > 85% for 10m -> page.
  - Pending queue > 100 for 5m -> page.
  - New AMI failing smoke tests in image pipeline -> block releases.

Operational hygiene & team wiki guidance

- Code ownership: Every module must have a CODEOWNERS entry and an owner in the module README.
- Changelog: All changes to modules must include a short CHANGELOG.md entry in the same PR.
- Runbook updates: If you change a production-facing step, update this playbook and add a reviewers check before merge.
- Communication: Significant infra changes (capacity > 10% or public network changes) require a pre-announce in #platform-updates and an RFC to eng-arch.

Oncall & escalation

- First responder: GPU-Fleet-Oncall (PagerDuty).
- Escalation: if issue not acknowledged in 10m, page eng-sre lead.
- Out-of-hours runbook: small scale operations (scale +/- 10%) may be performed by oncall. Changes > 10% require follow-up in a business-hours window.

Appendices

A. Useful CLI snippets

- Terraform plan in CI style:
  `terraform plan -var-file=envs/prod.tfvars -input=false -out=tfplan`

- Drain and terminate node (k8s + AWS):
  `kubectl drain ip-10-0-12-34 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data && aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-0abcd1234`

B. Contact & resources

- PagerDuty: GPU-Fleet-Oncall.
- Slack: #infra-oncall, #platform-updates.
- Repos: git@internal-repo:infra/modules.git, git@internal-repo:infra/terraform-consumers.git.
- Documentation: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026

C. Change log (selected)

- 2025-09-15: Initial published playbook (S. Ramirez).
- 2026-02-10: Added CI gating for cost guardrails and updated overprovisioning strategy (reviewers: E. Cole, M. Singh).

If you are making a change to modules that affect runtime behavior, follow the Module review & release process above and notify the oncall channel at least 24 hours before production apply.
